name: llama.cpp
purpose: C/C++ inference engine for large language models using the ggml/GGUF format, with quantisation, CPU and GPU backends across many platforms, and an OpenAI-compatible server.
journalism_use_case: The foundation of any newsroom AI capability that must not send documents to a vendor: run a capable instruction model on your own hardware for summarisation, claim extraction, translation assistance or redaction detection, with leaked material never leaving the building.
pros: Makes local inference genuinely practical on ordinary hardware through aggressive quantisation — which is what turns 'we should process this locally' into something that finishes
OpenAI-compatible server means tools written against hosted APIs (kuroi, Loki-style pipelines, your own code) can be pointed at your own model with a configuration change rather than a rewrite
MIT licensed with extraordinary activity (135,527 stars, v1.0.0 released 2026-11-13, pushed 2026-11-17) and backends for CPU, CUDA, Metal, Vulkan and more
Single binary with no Python dependency, so it deploys on a hardened or air-gapped machine where a framework install is impractical
cons: Fast-moving with frequent breaking changes in quantisation formats and server APIs, so pinning is essential and upgrades need testing — the 1.0.0 release is recent and the history before it was volatile
Quantisation costs quality in ways that vary by model and task, and the loss is rarely measured by the people deploying it — a quantised model that summarises badly will do so plausibly
Engineer-facing: you supply the model, choose the quantisation and operate the server, and model selection has more effect on output quality than anything the engine does
Running a local model does not make its output reliable: hallucination is a property of the model, and local deployment removes the privacy problem without touching the accuracy one
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 135,527 stars with release v1.0.0 (2026-11-13) and a push on 2026-11-17, MIT licence. Its role as the standard local-inference engine is verifiable from the ecosystem built on it, including Ollama and most desktop LLM applications.
assessment: Adopt it as the inference layer for every AI capability you want without a vendor — this is the single component that makes local AI a realistic newsroom choice. For your profile the right pattern is one GPU host running llama.cpp's OpenAI-compatible server, with every internal tool pointed at it, so the decision 'does this document leave the building' is made once in infrastructure rather than repeatedly by users. Pin the version, and evaluate your chosen quantisation on real tasks rather than assuming parity with the full model.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.0.0 (2026-11-13), 135,527 stars. Same-day commits at very high velocity with a newly reached 1.0; the maintenance concern is churn, not neglect.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the engine. Model weights carry their own licences, which vary enormously — this is where the licence risk in local AI actually sits.
licence_restrictions: Engine unrestricted. The engine licence does not launder a restricted model licence: running a non-commercial or restricted-weights model locally is still bound by those weights' terms.
costs: No fee. The cost is hardware: a GPU with sufficient VRAM for your chosen model (or substantial RAM for CPU inference at lower speed). One shared GPU host serves a small newsroom. Estimate; assumes self-hosted.
privacy: Entirely local inference with no telemetry and no external calls — the whole point. Model weights are downloaded once and can be pre-staged for air-gapped operation.
alternatives: Ollama for a much easier operational wrapper around the same engine
vLLM where GPU throughput for many concurrent requests matters more than footprint
Hosted model APIs — appropriate only for non-sensitive material
summary: C/C++ inference engine for large language models using the ggml/GGUF format, with quantisation…

name: Ollama
purpose: Application that packages local model serving behind a simple CLI and HTTP API, handling model download, quantisation selection, memory management and concurrent requests, with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
journalism_use_case: The practical way to give a newsroom local AI: one command installs it, one command pulls a model, and every internal tool has an OpenAI-compatible endpoint on the local network — which is the difference between local AI being a project and being available.
pros: Removes essentially all operational friction from local inference: model management, memory handling and serving are automatic, which is why it has become the default
OpenAI-compatible API means existing tools work unchanged, so you can redirect a pipeline from a hosted provider to local inference by changing a base URL
MIT licensed with enormous adoption (187,366 stars) and a very fast release cadence (v0.40.16, 2026-11-09; pushed 2026-11-17)
Cross-platform desktop and server support, so a reporter can run a model on a laptop and the newsroom can run one on a server with the same interface
cons: Abstracts away quantisation and model-variant choices, which is convenient and means teams often do not know which quantisation they are running — and that affects output quality materially

Model library convenience encourages pulling models without checking their licences: the library includes weights with restrictive terms alongside permissive ones, and the pull command does not make you read them
Fast release cadence with occasional behavioural changes, so pin the version for anything production
Defaults are tuned for convenience rather than for maximum throughput or minimum memory; a heavily used server benefits from vLLM or direct llama.cpp tuning
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 187,366 stars with release v0.40.16 (2026-11-09) and a push on 2026-11-17, MIT licence. Its position as the default local-model runner is evident from adoption scale.
assessment: Adopt it — the usability gain is what actually gets local AI deployed, and deployment is the point. For your profile two governance items matter more than the technology. First, record which model and quantisation each workflow uses, because 'we summarised with a local model' is not a reproducible methodology. Second, check the licence of every model you pull: the convenience of `ollama pull` is exactly how a non-commercial-weights model ends up behind a published story.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v0.40.16 (2026-11-09), 187,366 stars, MIT licence. Same-day commits with near-weekly releases and commercial backing.
model_or_data_licence: VARIES AND MATTERS: models in the library carry their own licences, from Apache-2.0 and MIT through to restrictive community licences with usage conditions. Verify each model you pull.
licence_restrictions: Application unrestricted. The real exposure is model licences, which `ollama pull` does not surface prominently — a commercially operated newsroom must check each model's terms before output reaches publication.
costs: No fee. Hardware is the cost: a GPU host for useful speed on larger models, or a capable laptop for small ones. One shared server serves a small newsroom. Estimate.
privacy: Local inference with no document content leaving your infrastructure. Model pulls contact Ollama's registry, which discloses which models you fetch (not your data) and can be pre-staged for air-gapped use.
alternatives: llama.cpp directly for control over quantisation and server behaviour
vLLM for high-throughput GPU serving
Hosted APIs for non-sensitive work only
blockers: Model licences in the library vary and are easy to overlook — verify before publishing work derived from a pulled model
summary: Application that packages local model serving behind a simple CLI and HTTP API, handling model download, quantisation selection…

name: vLLM
purpose: High-throughput LLM inference and serving engine using paged attention and continuous batching, with an OpenAI-compatible API and support for many model architectures and quantisation schemes.
journalism_use_case: Serving a local model to a whole newsroom or processing a large document corpus: continuous batching means dozens of concurrent requests or a million-document extraction job complete in a fraction of the time a single-stream engine would take.
pros: Throughput is the decisive advantage: for corpus-scale work (extracting entities or claims across a whole leak) vLLM's batching is the difference between days and hours on the same GPU
OpenAI-compatible server, so it drops into the same architecture as Ollama or llama.cpp with better scaling characteristics
Apache-2.0 under PyTorch Foundation governance with enormous activity (97,101 stars, v0.34.0 released 2026-11-16, pushed 2026-11-17)
Required by several document tools in this catalogue (Marker, Surya, olmOCR), so you may need it regardless
cons: GPU-only and VRAM-hungry: it is server infrastructure, not something that runs on a reporter's laptop, so it complements rather than replaces llama.cpp
Operationally heavier than Ollama — model loading, memory configuration and version-to-model compatibility all need attention, and mismatches fail confusingly
Very fast release cadence with a large surface, so pinning and testing are necessary; model-architecture support changes between versions
Python/CUDA dependency stack is the usual source of deployment pain, particularly in reproducible or air-gapped setups
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 97,101 stars with release v0.34.0 (2026-11-16) and a push on 2026-11-17, Apache-2.0 under PyTorch Foundation governance. Its use as the inference backend for Marker, Surya and olmOCR is verifiable from those projects' documentation.
assessment: Adopt it where you have GPUs and either concurrency or corpus scale — that is the specific case it wins, and it wins decisively. For your profile the clean architecture is vLLM on the GPU server for batch and shared use, Ollama or llama.cpp on laptops for individual work, and the same OpenAI-compatible interface everywhere so tools do not care which they are talking to. Note that several document tools here require it, which may settle the decision for you.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v0.34.0 (2026-11-16), 97,101 stars, Apache-2.0. Same-day commits and releases under foundation governance with broad industry contribution.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the server; model weights carry their own licences.
licence_restrictions: Server unrestricted. Model licence obligations apply independently.
costs: No fee. GPU hardware or rental is the cost and it is the dominant one — a capable GPU host is the main AI infrastructure line in a newsroom budget. Estimate; assumes self-hosted.
privacy: Local serving with no external calls; documents stay on your infrastructure. Model weights downloaded once and pre-stageable.
alternatives: Ollama for simpler operation at lower throughput
llama.cpp for CPU and laptop deployment
SGLang as an alternative high-throughput server
summary: High-throughput LLM inference and serving engine using paged attention and continuous batching…

name: LlamaIndex
purpose: Data framework for retrieval-augmented generation: loaders for many sources, index structures, retrievers, rerankers, query engines and agent abstractions over document collections.
journalism_use_case: Building a question-answering interface over a document archive: a reporter asks 'what did the ministry say about the contract in 2019' and the system retrieves relevant passages and drafts an answer with citations back to specific documents. The citation requirement is what makes it usable in journalism at all.
pros: Citation-aware retrieval is the feature that matters: an answer with document and page references can be checked, and an answer without them cannot be used in journalism
Very large loader ecosystem, so getting a corpus into an index is usually configuration rather than code
MIT licensed with enormous activity (52,926 stars, v0.14.26 released 2026-11-13, pushed 2026-11-14) and a well-funded maintainer
Pluggable at every layer, so the whole pipeline — embeddings, vector store, model — can be local
cons: Abstraction churn is real: the framework has repeatedly reorganised its APIs and package structure, so code written a year ago often needs rewriting, and tutorials age badly

RAG output remains model output: retrieved context reduces hallucination without eliminating it, and a confidently wrong answer with correct-looking citations is the characteristic failure mode — which is more dangerous in journalism than no answer
Commercial company behind it with a hosted platform, so some convenient paths lead to paid services and feature direction follows the business
Easy to build something impressive and unreliable: the framework makes a demo trivial and a trustworthy system hard, and the gap is mostly evaluation work it does not do for you
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 52,926 stars with release v0.14.26 (2026-11-13), pushed 2026-11-14, MIT licence. The API-churn pattern is visible in the project's own migration documentation across major versions.
assessment: Use it, with an evaluation discipline attached: build a set of questions with known correct answers from your own corpus and measure retrieval and answer quality before anyone relies on the system. For your profile the architecture to insist on is fully local (local embeddings, local vector store, local model via vLLM) and citation-mandatory — an answer without a document reference should be suppressed rather than shown. Pin the version; this framework breaks across upgrades more than most.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v0.14.26 (2026-11-13), 52,926 stars, MIT licence. Very frequent releases under commercial maintenance; the churn that follows is the practical cost.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the framework; embedding models, rerankers and LLMs carry their own licences.
licence_restrictions: Framework unrestricted. Imported licence risk from the models you configure, and the hosted LlamaCloud platform operates under separate commercial terms.
costs: Framework free. Costs are the model and embedding infrastructure (a GPU host) or, if you configure hosted providers, their per-token charges (not priced here). Estimate.
privacy: Can be fully local, and for source material must be: the default convenience path uses hosted embedding and LLM providers, which would send your documents to them. Configure local components deliberately and verify no fallback to a hosted default.
alternatives: Haystack for a more stable, production-oriented RAG framework
txtai for a lighter all-in-one option
Direct retrieval plus a prompt, which for many newsroom cases is sufficient and far more transparent
blockers: Default configurations use hosted embedding and model providers — must be explicitly made local for source material
summary: Data framework for retrieval-augmented generation: loaders for many sources, index structures, retrievers, rerankers…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure

name: Haystack
purpose: Framework for building search and RAG pipelines from composable components — retrievers, rankers, readers, generators, document stores — with an explicit pipeline graph and evaluation tooling.
journalism_use_case: The same document question-answering capability as LlamaIndex, built on an explicit pipeline graph that is easier to reason about and test — which matters when the system will inform reporting and you must be able to explain and audit what it does.
pros: Explicit pipeline composition makes the system auditable: you can see and test each stage, which is substantially better for a journalism application than a framework that hides retrieval behind convenience methods
Built-in evaluation components, so measuring retrieval and answer quality is part of the framework rather than an afterthought — the discipline journalism actually needs
Apache-2.0 with a clear 3.x release line (v3.5.0, 2026-11-10; pushed 2026-11-17) and a company with a long record in open-source NLP search
Document-store abstraction supports local options (OpenSearch, Qdrant, in-memory), so a fully local deployment is a first-class path rather than a workaround
cons: Smaller community than LlamaIndex (27,027 stars), so there are fewer third-party integrations and less material to copy from
Major-version transitions (1.x to 2.x to 3.x) have required rewrites, so it is not immune to the churn that affects this whole category
Commercial company behind it with a hosted platform, the usual open-core consideration for feature direction
Still a RAG framework: it improves auditability but does not solve hallucination, and a well-built Haystack pipeline can still produce a confident wrong answer
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 27,027 stars with release v3.5.0 (2026-11-10), pushed 2026-11-17, Apache-2.0. deepset's longer history in open-source NLP search predates the current RAG wave, which is relevant context for the engineering approach.
assessment: My preferred RAG framework for your context, on auditability grounds: the explicit pipeline and built-in evaluation match what journalism requires from an AI component — the ability to say what it does and how well it does it. For your profile I would build the archive question-answering system on Haystack with local components throughout, invest early in an evaluation set from your own documents, and treat the output as a research aid that always shows its sources.

additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure

name: RAGFlow
purpose: Deployable RAG platform with deep document understanding, a web interface for corpus management and chat, visual chunking inspection, citation display and agent workflows.
journalism_use_case: Giving reporters a working document-chat interface without building one: deploy RAGFlow, upload a corpus, and a journalist can ask questions and see which passages the answer came from — with the chunking visible, so you can diagnose why a bad answer happened.
pros: A complete product rather than a framework: reporters get a usable interface immediately, which is the gap between RAG as an engineering project and RAG as a newsroom tool
Visible chunking and citation display are genuinely well judged for this use case — being able to see what the system retrieved is how a journalist decides whether to trust an answer
Apache-2.0 with very large adoption (94,307 stars), a 1.0 release (2026-11-06) and same-day commits, plus an almost empty issue tracker
Self-hostable with local model support, so the whole system can stay inside the perimeter
cons: Heavy multi-service deployment (document parsing, vector store, web application, workers), so it is a platform commitment comparable to OpenAleph rather than a quick install
Commercial company behind it with a hosted offering, so open-version feature boundaries warrant checking before you depend on something

The polished interface invites uncritical use: a reporter seeing a fluent cited answer may not check the citations, which makes editorial guidance more important than with a developer-facing framework
Deep-document-understanding components may pull models whose licences need verification, and the convenience of the pipeline obscures what is being used
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 94,307 stars with only 9 open issues, release v1.0.0 (2026-11-06), pushed 2026-11-17, Apache-2.0. The adoption scale and near-empty tracker are both notable; the hosted-offering relationship is documented by the vendor.
assessment: Pilot it if you want reporters to have document chat and can support the deployment — it is the most complete self-hostable option and the citation visibility is the right design. For your profile the controls that matter are editorial rather than technical: train reporters that the citation is the answer and the prose is a convenience, and audit a sample of answers against the underlying documents before the tool is trusted on a live investigation. Verify which models the parsing pipeline pulls.

model_or_data_licence: Embedded parsing and embedding models carry their own licences and were NOT individually verified in this survey.
licence_restrictions: Platform permissive. Verify the licences of bundled or auto-downloaded models before commercial publication of derived work.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: a multi-container deployment plus a vector store and a GPU for local models — comparable to running a search platform. Hosted option priced separately (not verified). Assumptions: self-hosted, moderate corpus.
privacy: Self-hostable with local models, which is the configuration to use for source material. Check that no component defaults to a hosted embedding or LLM provider.
alternatives: Haystack plus a simple interface for an auditable, engineer-controlled alternative
ICIJ Datashare or OpenAleph where search rather than generative answers is what reporters need
txtai for a much lighter semantic-search deployment

additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure

name: Qdrant
purpose: Vector similarity search engine and database written in Rust, with payload filtering, quantisation, snapshots, distributed deployment and a REST and gRPC API.
journalism_use_case: The storage layer for semantic search over a document archive: millions of passage embeddings with metadata filters, so a reporter can search semantically within a date range or a specific document set rather than across everything.
pros: Payload filtering combined with vector search is the feature that matters for investigative use: 'semantically similar passages, but only in documents from this ministry in 2019' is a normal journalistic query and a hard technical one
Rust implementation with quantisation support keeps memory requirements manageable at millions of vectors, which decides whether a corpus fits on your hardware
Apache-2.0 with very active maintenance (v1.20.2, 2026-11-16; pushed 2026-11-17) and strong adoption (35,603 stars)
Snapshots make the index backup-able and portable, which matters when the index represents substantial embedding compute
cons: Another stateful service to operate alongside whatever search engine you already run — and for many newsroom corpora, a vector extension in OpenSearch or pgvector avoids that
Commercial company with a managed cloud offering, the usual open-core direction consideration
Embedding storage is only as good as the embedding model, and switching models means re-embedding the entire corpus — a cost that is easy to underestimate when choosing a model
At small corpus sizes (tens of thousands of documents) a dedicated vector database is unnecessary overhead compared with FAISS or an in-memory index
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 35,603 stars with release v1.20.2 (2026-11-16) and a push on 2026-11-17, Apache-2.0. Strong adoption in the RAG ecosystem is evident from the metrics.
assessment: Adopt it when your corpus genuinely needs a vector database — millions of passages with filtered search — and use pgvector or FAISS below that threshold. For your profile the decision that costs most is the embedding model, not the database: choose it once with care (multilingual-e5-large is a reasonable default with a clear licence), because re-embedding a leak-scale corpus is days of GPU time. Keep the index on infrastructure you control.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.20.2 (2026-11-16), 35,603 stars, Apache-2.0. Same-day commits and frequent releases under well-funded commercial maintenance.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Embeddings are derived from your documents using a model whose licence applies to that use.
licence_restrictions: None material for the database. The managed cloud service is a separate commercial product.
costs: No fee for self-hosting. Infrastructure: RAM-proportional to vector count (quantisation reduces this substantially) plus disk — one VM for several million vectors. Managed cloud priced separately (not verified). Estimate.
privacy: Self-hosted, local, no external calls. The index itself is disclosive about your corpus, so it needs the same protection as the documents.
alternatives: pgvector if you already run PostgreSQL — usually the right answer below millions of vectors
FAISS for an in-process index with no service to operate
OpenSearch or Solr vector search if you already run one for keyword search
summary: Vector similarity search engine and database written in Rust, with payload filtering, quantisation, snapshots…

name: FAISS
purpose: Library for efficient similarity search and clustering of dense vectors, with many index types trading memory against accuracy and speed, and GPU acceleration.
journalism_use_case: In-process vector search with no service to run: embed a corpus, build a FAISS index, and query it from the same Python process — the right level of infrastructure for a single investigation's document set, and what sentence-transformers examples assume.
pros: No service to operate: an index is a file and a process, which suits per-investigation corpora and air-gapped machines where running a database is impractical
Wide range of index types lets you trade memory for accuracy explicitly, which matters when a corpus must fit on available hardware
MIT licensed with very active maintenance (v1.16.0, 2026-11-10; pushed 2026-11-17) and long institutional backing (41,767 stars)
The reference implementation in this space, so its behaviour is well understood and widely documented
cons: No metadata filtering: FAISS searches vectors, so 'similar passages from 2019 only' requires filtering outside the index, which is awkward and slow at scale — Qdrant's main advantage
No persistence model beyond saving index files, so updates, deletions and incremental additions need application-level handling
Library-level: there is no API, no auth and no multi-user access, so sharing search with reporters means building something around it
Index-type selection and training parameters materially affect recall, and a badly configured index silently misses results — which in investigative search is the dangerous failure
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 41,767 stars with release v1.16.0 (2026-11-10) and a push on 2026-11-17, MIT licence. Its status as the standard vector-search library is evident from its use across the ecosystem including txtai and sentence-transformers examples.
assessment: Adopt it for per-investigation corpora and scripted analysis, and move to Qdrant or pgvector when you need filtering, persistence or multi-user access. For your profile the practical warning is recall: an approximate index can silently omit relevant passages, so for completeness-sensitive work either use an exact index (feasible for modest corpora) or pair semantic search with keyword search and tell reporters that neither alone is exhaustive.

costs: No fee. RAM proportional to vectors and index type; GPU optional. No service infrastructure. Estimate.
privacy: In-process and local; index files stay with you. Suitable for air-gapped work.
